title: The Other Door of the Theatre
memory_text: Leonie led me through the theatre by the door ordinarily used for scenery, not by the splendid entrance at which the patrons congratulated themselves for attending art. A young draughtsman was measuring the side flats with a carpenter's rule. Theodor Vahl had ink on his cuff and a way of listening which made my more elaborate remarks sound, for once, like a waste of the listener's time. When I said the false perspective was wrong, he asked for the distance from which I intended to view it. We spent the evening moving a lamp by inches and watching painted columns become convincing. His fingers were stained blue from the pigments; mine from the laboratory. He proposed that we exchange notebooks, an offer sufficiently improper to interest me. Leonie warned that he kept drawings better than he kept appointments. On my departure Theodor handed me a sketch of the lamp's position. He had put my name under the diagram, an unnecessary courtesy which I nevertheless examined twice before filing it. I returned to the theatre three evenings later to correct a measurement I had already checked.

title: A Walk That Was Not an Experiment
memory_text: Theodor asked me to walk with him after the last performance. I assumed he wished to discuss the problem of reflected light, for which I had brought notes. Instead he bought two paper cones of roasted chestnuts and directed us toward the river. The air smelled of wet stone and spent coal. We spoke first of the new bridge, then of his mother, who believed a draughtsman should seek employment more regular than a theatre. I offered an admirably detailed argument against maternal interference. He laughed and said that I had mistaken a complaint for a question. We reached the bend in the embankment before I noticed he had carried my notebook under his arm all the way from the theatre. When I took it back our hands remained together a moment longer than the exchange required. I have made a good many measurements of hesitation since then. None has been as irritating to recall as that one. We returned separately through different streets, though no law compelled us to do so. One must allow for the appetite of neighbors.

title: The Door Left Unlatched
memory_text: Theodor's room contained a narrow bed, three portfolios and a perpetually inadequate stove. He had borrowed a lens from me to enlarge a stage design, and I went to retrieve it after supper. He had left the door unlatched because, he said, I knocked as though serving a writ. There was a bottle of ordinary red wine on the sill. We argued about whether the painted moon on a backdrop should be allowed to cast an impossible shadow. I finally kissed him to interrupt his objection. The objection resumed afterward, rather to my delight. He did not ask me to give this occurrence a name. When I left, I forgot the lens and took his scarf instead. Leonie noticed it around my neck the next morning, advised me that its color was unforgiving, and continued sewing without requiring an explanation. I resented her discretion almost as much as I benefited from it. Theodor kept the lens for another month. It produced an excellent drawing. I have never decided which of us was most pleased with the arrangement.

title: A Table Set for Three
memory_text: Clara invited us to supper and laid three places without commentary upon the hour at which Theodor and I arrived together. There was cabbage, a small roast and bread too coarse for a respectable faculty dinner. Theodor supplied a story about a painted waterfall that collapsed during a performance. I improved the story by explaining why the failure had been predictable. Clara told me that the failure was not the point. They continued their conversation around me while I ate in injured silence. Afterward she gave Theodor a wrapped parcel of biscuits and asked whether he had enough coal. She asked me whether I had finally repaired the cabinet catch. It took me several days to decide that she had treated us differently, and somewhat longer to realize why. Theodor said that she understood affection well enough not to make an exhibition of it. I said that she was a woman of sound practical instincts. He replied that this was the longest possible way of admitting agreement.

title: The Photograph Not Taken
memory_text: On an excursion to Augsburg, Theodor proposed a photograph. The operator had arranged a velvet chair and two potted palms as though respectable companionship could be manufactured out of upholstery. I would not sit beside Theodor for the proposed double portrait. The operator had already asked which of us was the elder brother, and I disliked the readiness with which a stranger sought a category for us. Theodor offered to stand behind the chair, his hand on its carved back. I declined that too. We were photographed separately. In his portrait his hair refuses to lie flat over the left ear; in mine I look as though I had been ordered to attend my own memorial service. Theodor paid for both and said very little on the train. I told myself I had resisted vulgar sentimentality. In my pocket was a receipt for two photographs, and on the reverse he had written the time our train arrived. I still possess that receipt. The portraits were never placed together in a frame.

title: A Place beside the Window
memory_text: Following my appointment, I bought a respectable writing table and transferred the specimens from the window shelf to a locked cupboard. Theodor came to see the changes and stood looking at the clear space where his portfolio had formerly rested. He congratulated me on the appointment without enthusiasm. I told him that faculty rooms required arrangement and that the drawings would be safer elsewhere. He said he had not asked whether they were safe. I answered with an account of the risks attached to loose papers and spilled reagents. We ate cold meat while the new table occupied half the room between us. Before leaving he set a wooden ruler beside the window, precisely where it had always lain. A week later I moved it to a drawer to make room for an anatomical plate. The ruler remained there through the entire winter, although I used inferior instruments rather than fetch it. Had I been asked at the time, I should have insisted the matter concerned only furniture.

title: A Sunday without the Laboratory
memory_text: Theodor obtained a Sunday free from work and asked me to travel out to a country inn. He had brought a small bag containing bread, pears and the drawing he wished to show me. I arrived two hours late with a bottle of preserved tissue wrapped in my coat. He did not immediately speak. We took a table outdoors. His drawing showed the theatre wall after rain, its plaster cracking in slow curves. I described the bottle's unusual response to temperature before I had properly looked at his work. He folded the paper. I offered to explain that my experiment might fail altogether if left overnight. He said, quietly, that the experiments were always at the point of failure and there would never be a day sufficiently unimportant to keep free. I replied that he had chosen a profession in which performances also dictated one's hours. He said that performances ended. I remember the pears more clearly than the journey home. One had bruised in the bag and we cut away the black portion with his penknife. Neither of us called the afternoon a quarrel. We knew perfectly well that it was one.

title: The Drawing Returned
memory_text: Theodor received an offer to prepare architectural drawings in another city. I met him at Leonie's workroom, where half-completed costumes hung like people unwilling to commit themselves to a profession. He showed me the terms of employment. They were good, although not so good that I could not find objections. He asked whether I wished him to decline. The room contained an empty chair and a bowl of pins. I considered telling him that the laboratory would soon produce results worth witnessing. Instead I explained that advancement ought not to be sacrificed to an arrangement whose terms neither of us had properly established. He repeated the word arrangement as though testing a badly made hinge. He returned my lens wrapped in the theatre drawing on which we had first disagreed. I congratulated him on his future and left before Leonie could introduce sympathy into the discussion. Three months later I discovered that I had been consulting his notes on perspective while marking an anatomical proof. His absence had become useful to me as an excuse for a number of errors which were wholly mine.

title: A Pamphlet Read Twice
memory_text: I read one of Karl Heinrich Ulrichs's tracts in a Munich printer's waiting room in 1867. Its arguments about men whose affections turned toward men were expressed with a lawyer's appetite for categories, several of which I found biologically unpersuasive. Yet the candor of the enterprise was remarkable. He did not petition for a toleration disguised as illness; he demanded that the law explain its own jurisdiction. I made notes in the margin, then tore them out because I had written upon a borrowed copy. A printer's assistant asked whether I knew the author's work. I said that I knew an argument when I saw one, regardless of its author's domestic arrangements. It was a clever answer and a cowardly one, a combination in which I had lately become proficient. I bought another copy before leaving. I did not meet Ulrichs and have no right to borrow his courage for my own account. His printed words did, however, make a question I had considered private appear on a public page.

title: The New Offence
locations: Tower kitchen and Ingolstadt post office
memory_text: The new imperial criminal code arrived in the district wrapped in all the language of administrative progress. Paragraph 175 was short enough to fit upon a scrap of paper. I copied its wording and placed the copy beside an older Bavarian legal digest, then spent the afternoon demonstrating to Clara that an empire could take an act previously outside that particular criminal prohibition and manufacture an offender by printing a sentence. She replied that a gentleman with a tower could afford certain sorts of indignation more readily than a clerk with a family. At the post office a man was asked, within my hearing, why he received so many letters from the same address. Nothing came of the question. I remembered it nevertheless. That evening I sealed a letter to Theodor, intending only to tell him of the changed statute. I did not post it. I was angry at the law, and somewhat angrier that my first impulse had been to imagine my old companion in danger, rather than to ask whether he was content.

title: The Borrowed Name
memory_text: Mathilde introduced me to Max Reiss, a schoolteacher who wished to have a short defense of a dismissed colleague printed without identifying the author. Reiss was careful with his verbs and almost reckless with the number of copies he proposed to circulate. I asked whether the colleague had broken the law. He said that he did not know, and that the allegation had preceded any examination. Mathilde declined to print a name without the man's consent. I proposed a general argument about accusations unsupported by evidence and spent three nights correcting it. Reiss thought the piece too cold to influence the public. Mathilde said that my colder language might keep the teacher employed. We printed fewer copies than Reiss wanted. Weeks later he reported that the school had quietly ceased asking questions. I claimed no victory; no public correction had appeared. What I retained was Mathilde's insistence that the person concerned should choose how much of himself the pamphlet spent.

title: The Gentleman Who Was Not My Type
memory_text: Reiss introduced me to a retired merchant at an outdoor table. The gentleman's chief intellectual accomplishment was the possession of a watch which chimed a quarter-hour inaccurately. He was also plainly interested in my company, an interest communicated through attentions too numerous to mistake. I attempted an elaborate description of my microscopic work to discourage him. Reiss watched the performance with visible amusement. On the way back he said I could simply have declined an invitation. I answered that plain refusal was frequently mistaken for an insult. Reiss said that my alternative had been an insult with diagrams. I considered whether the man's attention had displeased me because it was unwanted or because I disliked being seen to receive it. These were different questions. I did not settle either. At our next meeting I spoke to the merchant courteously, and he discovered my research tedious. We parted on terms that would have been difficult to improve through further analysis.

title: The Letter with the Familiar Hand
memory_text: A letter from Theodor arrived after years in which our correspondence had dwindled to notes at Christmas. He had secured a position supervising architectural drawings and was living with a man whose patience, he said, exceeded that of most professors. The sentence was not an accusation, though I spent a whole afternoon searching it for one. He enclosed a photograph of a building whose windows he had designed. It was handsome and insufficiently ventilated. I prepared a reply listing the defect, then put the sheet away. Clara, bringing fresh cloth for the jars, found me looking at the picture. I told her that the work was competently done. She asked whether I had said as much to him. I wrote him three sentences of praise and an additional paragraph about the windows. He answered in kind, correcting a detail I had misunderstood about the plan. We had lost the ease of our earlier life. We had not lost the pleasure of being exact together.

title: A Bed for a Visitor
memory_text: Reiss came to the tower with a damaged valise and asked whether he might stay two nights while a difficult question was settled at his school. I gave him the west room, chiefly because it was the only chamber in which the roof was not leaking. He told me an acquaintance had threatened to expose the correspondence between himself and another man. I asked whether the letters were authentic. He said they were. I advised him not to purchase silence from someone who could demand further payment. He pointed out that I possessed a locked gate, independent income sufficient for my habits, and almost no institutional reputation left to lose. He did not. I sent Mathilde a note asking her to retain his papers in a sealed envelope, should he choose to deposit them. Reiss went away without using the offer. For weeks afterward I checked the west-room window latch before bed, although the room was empty. I did not regard myself as responsible for his security. The latch received considerable attention nevertheless.

title: Not a Patient
memory_text: A physician acquaintance asked whether I thought the attachments of men such as Reiss could be described as a nervous disorder. Reiss himself was absent. I refused the premise that his life could be converted into a case study merely because he was not there to interrupt us. Reuter asked, reasonably, whether my objections were scientific or personal. I said that a diagnosis required a defined pathological process, not an offended audience. He brought several contemporary works on the matter; I read them and found the authors capable of observing great detail while committing themselves prematurely to explanation. I did not therefore conclude that all men who desired men resembled one another, still less that each man must live by a single new label. That evening I attempted a study of the Queen's appetite and found her unusually indifferent to my arrangement. I recorded the result without inventing a syndrome of disobedience. I congratulate myself, perhaps extravagantly, on having learned at least one lesson about the difference between behavior and disease.

title: A Page Torn from the Programme
memory_text: Leonie sent me a theatre programme annotated with a request that I attend a performance by two visiting musicians. Reiss met me at the side entrance. Inside, one musician played too rapidly and the other watched him with a concentration I recognized. During the interval Reiss asked whether I was enjoying myself. I said that the second player could have selected a stronger partner. He suggested that musical partnership was not always chosen by a committee of critics. On the reverse of the programme Leonie had sketched an absurd crown and written, 'Try staying until the end.' I stayed. The musicians made several errors together and recovered without a signal from the audience. Afterward Reiss invited me for a late supper with friends. I declined, citing the state of the laboratory, though the experiment could have been abandoned without loss. On the walk home I found that I could reproduce both players' mistakes. I could not reproduce the ordinary courage with which they had continued.

title: No Properly Named Relation
memory_text: Reiss wished to leave the region for a post in Switzerland. Mathilde prepared a bill for the pamphlets we had printed years before, although she knew he had no intention of settling it that day. He asked whether I would write a recommendation. I pointed out that I had been removed from a faculty and my authority was consequently of questionable value. He said my judgment had not been formally dismissed with me. I wrote the letter without mentioning his private life, which was none of the receiving institution's concern. Reiss looked at the seal and asked whether we had been friends. I said that friendship was a dangerously elastic word, stretched over acquaintances, debtors, conspirators and people who shared an inconvenient table. He said he would take that as yes. I did not correct him. His last letter from abroad described snow on the window frame and an unusually good class of students. The handwriting was smaller than before. Mathilde left his unpaid bill in the drawer rather than sending it after him.

title: An Instrument and Its Keeper
memory_text: Adler returned to Mathilde's shop with the disputed lens and a scrap of cloth protecting its rim. He had brought its maker's mark into better light by cleaning away a century of accumulated polish. I praised the work, then questioned his method with enough severity to suggest the result had injured me. Julian refused to take offense. He placed the lens in my hand and told me to examine the new reflection rather than his character. I watched him pack his tools, arranging each in a leather sleeve cut precisely to its size. He had a scar along one knuckle; it appeared when he bent his fingers around the case latch. I asked about it. He said the workshop had been careless with a press. I found the scar more difficult to disregard than the instrument. Mathilde later said that I had become uncommonly attentive to the condition of other people's hands. I informed her that a craftsman's hands were an essential part of his apparatus, which was both accurate and not the entire explanation.

title: The Words in the Margin
memory_text: A volume of German commentary on friendship arrived from Julian with two passages marked in pencil. The first concerned the intimacy of men whose work required perfect trust. The second, less conveniently, concerned the forms of affection which custom made difficult to describe. I placed it beneath a stack of botanical catalogues until Voss arrived to retrieve her papers. She noticed the volume and remarked that a man who collected such a quantity of print could hardly object when the printed world described him. I told her that literature routinely mistook strong collaboration for sentiment. She asked which passage had compelled the complaint. I sent Julian a technical objection, twenty lines long, to the editor's translation. He answered with an account of how he had repaired the book's broken spine and added, 'I did not send it for the editor.' I read the sentence after supper and then again in the morning. I replied without discussing the second passage. Some invitations are most revealing in the care one expends pretending not to recognize them.

title: A Room without Witnesses
memory_text: I was in Vienna for three days and spent the second evening at Julian's rooms, where the stove made a noise like a distant carriage. He had set out simple bread, cold fish and a small bottle of wine. We disputed the merits of a German translation until the clock struck two. He took the glass from my hand before I spilled it on his notes. I put my hand over his, not to reclaim the glass. He remained still. I kissed him; he returned the kiss, and for once neither of us attempted to improve the moment by speaking. We stayed together that night. In the morning the bread had gone stale, my waistcoat was draped over the chair, and his injured hand required time before it could manage the buttons of his shirt. I fastened one for him. He asked whether I would stay another day. I said I had a train and work waiting. He did not ask me to defend my priorities. I gave him the train's departure time and, without being asked, the date I expected to return. That addition has survived in my memory longer than the argument which preceded it.

title: The Agreement We Did Not Sign
memory_text: Julian proposed that we agree upon what our acquaintance meant. He was not asking for an oath, still less a public announcement, but he wished to know whether my arrivals and departures belonged to a shared arrangement or merely to my convenience. I reminded him that my research could not be suspended for the sake of domestic regularity. He said he had never asked it to be. I then accused him of expecting an affection that could be scheduled. This was an answer to a question he had not put. Finally he said that he wanted to be free to accept another companion without committing a breach of a promise I refused to name. The possibility annoyed me more than it had any right to do. I declared that he was entirely at liberty. I continued stirring my cold coffee after the sugar had dissolved. He said that freedom offered with visible resentment was still freedom, but hardly a generous gift. We parted with a handshake in the crowded room. I disliked his correctness most of all because it did not make him less desirable.

title: A Letter That Was His
memory_text: I had already offended Voss by opening a letter Julian addressed to her. My explanation about shared correspondence was ingenious and unconvincing. Julian wrote separately to say that Voss had asked for an instrument drawing and that he intended to treat her request without my supervision. The paper bore the same careful hand I knew from his catalogues, but no familiar flourish at the close. I began a reply accusing him of making a principle out of a clerical oversight. Instead I sent a short acknowledgment, and a second envelope containing the diagram I had withheld in case he should require it. Weeks later Voss returned from travel and found my desk cleared of the offending letters. She did not thank me. She said that trust between adults was not a cabinet to which one man issued the keys. I told her she had selected an elaborate metaphor. I had, however, ceased opening her post. Julian sent a technical correction the next month, and I read it without looking for an accusation between its measurements.
prior_expectations: Concern for access to Julian entitled me to read others' letters
observations: The correspondence concerned Voss and an instrument, not me
decisions: I apologized through corrected behavior and unobtrusive assistance
consequences: Respect for separate relationships became testable
belief_changes: The other's privacy could be a real boundary
relationship_changes: Julian and Voss retained an independent bond despite my interference

title: A Visit Not Entirely Scientific
memory_text: Julian arrived unexpectedly with a small chest of instrument parts, and I nearly concealed my pleasure by accusing him of failing to announce the journey. He said he had already written; the letter was in my pocket. Leonie, who was visiting with a parcel of black cloth, greeted him as though she had long expected our paths to become indistinguishable. That evening Julian helped fit a shutter in the south room. I instructed him in the operation of the hinges and he reminded me that he had repaired more delicate machinery before breakfast. When Leonie left, she touched his sleeve and told him to insist upon supper before allowing me another demonstration. She did not treat him as a secret or a spectacle. The following morning I discovered that Julian had left a folded square of cloth beside my cup to protect the table from a leaking reagent bottle. I placed it there again after washing it. I had contrived no new discovery during his visit. Nevertheless the hours were not, by any sensible reckoning, lost.

observations: Julian came without demanding display and participated in ordinary labor
decisions: I shared the evening and kept his table cloth
consequences: I made room for companionship without converting it into a specimen
belief_changes: Unproductive time could still possess value
relationship_changes: Leonie tacitly acknowledged and accommodated the bond

title: The Newspaper from London
memory_text: News of Oscar Wilde's conviction reached us through the foreign papers. Mathilde laid a report upon her table and said that a man's entire life could be reduced to the word assigned him by a court. Julian had heard of the case before me. He seemed chiefly offended by the delight with which observers converted private correspondence into public entertainment. I examined the English statute and the reports as far as they were available, and found the legal machinery both efficient and indecently proud of itself. There were choices in the celebrated man's conduct which I did not admire. That did not make the state's right to arrange his humiliations self-evident. Julian asked whether I felt safe in Bavaria. I answered that safety was not an intellectual virtue. He said he had not asked whether it was virtuous. I changed the subject to a cracked prism. The discussion ended there, but I kept the newspaper folded among my scientific correspondence rather than with theatrical gossip. It was a reminder that observers do not require accuracy when they have found a spectacle that pleases them.

observations: Wilde's trial converted private life into public spectacle
decisions: I examined legal reports and kept the clipping
consequences: Threat became historical and immediate rather than abstract
belief_changes: A legal conviction is not a scientific or moral explanation
relationship_changes: Julian's concern about safety met my defensive rhetoric

title: His Work on the Wall
memory_text: Julian exhibited a restored measuring instrument without mentioning my assistance in identifying the original scale. I was vexed. He had not concealed my work out of malice; I had made no contribution to the restoration beyond supplying one diagram. Yet I had grown used to finding myself somewhere in the explanation of his achievements. When I approached the display he was speaking to a young maker whose hands shook with excitement. He introduced me as a colleague whose judgment had occasionally spared him expense, a description at once accurate and ungenerous to my vanity. Voss, beside me, asked what exactly I believed had been stolen. I said that a useful history should record every cause. She replied that this would require a book longer than the building. Julian came afterward and asked whether I liked the restoration. I did. We went to supper. I resisted the temptation to convert the evening into a hearing about the boundaries of influence, which he might reasonably have won.
prior_expectations: A partner's achievements ought naturally to acknowledge my contribution
observations: Julian's accomplishment stood independently
decisions: I accepted a proportionate acknowledgment and attended supper
consequences: A small exercise in reducing possessiveness succeeded
belief_changes: Shared life did not require shared authorship
relationship_changes: Julian retained professional autonomy without losing my company

title: Science and the Petition
memory_text: Mathilde showed me a notice of the campaign associated with Magnus Hirschfeld and the new Scientific-Humanitarian Committee. Reiss, writing from abroad, had enclosed a few observations about the circulation of Ulrichs's work. I recognized the ambition to place scientific evidence against a penal statute, although I disliked the confidence with which some writers believed a sufficiently neat explanation of desire would compel humane conduct. Scientists could supply facts; lawmakers might still choose to be cruel. Mathilde asked whether I would sign a petition. I said that I would first examine its wording, which was true. I then neglected the matter for several weeks, which was another truth and less dignified. When I finally sent my name, I did so through her, with a note correcting two technical statements in the accompanying appeal. She told me that signatures had been requested rather than a journal referee's report. I replied that both deserved scrutiny. I kept Reiss's letter with the copy of the statute from 1871, two papers sharing a drawer despite an interval of twenty-six years.

observations: Organized petitioning and community letters showed politics not reducible to evidence
decisions: I read, delayed and then signed with corrections
consequences: An act of solidarity occurred without a conversion narrative
belief_changes: Facts alone would not guarantee justice
relationship_changes: Mathilde and Reiss remained principled contacts across decades

title: The Terms of an Open Door
memory_text: Julian visited on his way through Bavaria, carrying no instrument at all. I regarded this as a disarming omission. We walked in the garden, where the nettles had appropriated a path I had intended to repair for years. He spoke of the life he had made in Vienna, of friends whose names were not familiar to me, and of a younger restorer to whom he had entrusted part of his business. I discovered that I had been treating his absence as a temporary condition which my next letter might end. He said he cared for me, but would not arrange his remaining years around a door which opened only when my experiments permitted. I objected to the theatricality of his metaphor and knew immediately that it was mine he had learned. He did not threaten to sever the connection. He asked only that I cease describing another person's independence as a betrayal. After his departure I had the neglected path cut back. I wrote to him describing the work, not pretending it had been done for an optical demonstration. He sent a short note asking whether the nettles would return. They have, repeatedly.
prior_expectations: A relationship could be resumed whenever my work allowed it
observations: Julian made an independent life and asked only honest terms
decisions: I cleared a path and wrote without invented technical necessity
consequences: Unresolved attachment persisted without a promised domestic future
belief_changes: Another's autonomy could not be filed under disloyalty
relationship_changes: Julian and I retained affection with a deliberately unsettled future
